e.t: This Hebrew word means “Lord” and functions as a respectful title for God in the Old Testament. It identifies the one addressed, spoken about, or appealed to as the supreme Lord. The word appears 445 times in the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis through Malachi, showing its broad use in prayer, prophetic speech, and declarations about God. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a title recognizing the Lord’s authority and identity.

The word means “high,” describing something positioned above others or standing at a great height. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is used for physical height, elevated places, and things or beings distinguished by their position above what surrounds them. Its basic function is descriptive: it tells the reader that something is high. It occurs 37 times in 32 verses, with usage spanning Genesis through Zephaniah and appearing across varied Old Testament settings.

Gozan is a proper name used for a place, rather than a general descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears five times and is consistently rendered “Gozan.” Its occurrences are found in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and Isaiah. The word functions as a place-name in passages referring to Gozan alongside other locations. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to “wheels,” the plural term for round, turning objects. In the Hebrew corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Daniel 7:9. Because no verse text or broader lexical definition is available, the safest explanation is this basic concrete meaning rather than assigning it a symbolic or theological sense. Its specific force in Daniel 7:9 must be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the word alone.

This Hebrew word commonly functions as “that,” helping connect words, phrases, or clauses within a sentence. It appears 347 times in the Hebrew Old Testament data, especially in Ezra and Daniel, so it serves a recurring connecting role rather than naming a person, object, or action. Its precise force depends on how it joins the surrounding words in each sentence.

Daniel is a personal name used to identify a particular man throughout the book of Daniel. It functions as a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs 52 times, all within Daniel, from Daniel 2:13 through 7:28. Its precise significance in any individual verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary role is simply to name Daniel.

It helps identify something as the one in view, whether near in the wording or made clear by the surrounding sentence. The word appears 1,178 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is a common way of directing attention to a specific subject. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “warm.” It describes a condition in which a person or thing is warm. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, making it an established word without being among the most frequent. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, since the available material does not include verse text. It can function within descriptions of warmth or becoming warm.

As a name, it identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The available wording does not establish an additional ordinary meaning for the name, so it is best understood simply as the person’s name in that passage. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding biblical context.

This Hebrew word functions as a verb meaning “were,” describing a past state or condition. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 25:18. Because it appears only once and no verse text is provided here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding context. Its basic contribution is to state that someone or something existed in a particular condition at a past time.

It identifies an individual in the Old Testament and occurs only once in the Hebrew corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:34. Because no broader definition or contextual verse text is available here, its secure ordinary sense is its function as a person’s name, not an expanded meaning or symbolic description.

This Hebrew word refers to “enemies”—those who stand against a person, people, or God’s purposes. It is used as a noun for an opposing party rather than for a general difficulty or problem. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 283 times, showing that opposition and enemies are recurring subjects in Israel’s history, worship, and prophetic writings. Its precise force in any passage depends on who is opposing whom and how the surrounding context describes that conflict.

Its scriptural connections place it in a statement involving speech, giving, and what a person did, reinforcing the idea of upright conduct recognized in a person’s life.

Chun is the name “Chun,” identifying a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. Canneh is a proper name for a place, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Scripture also uses it in settings involving commands and responses, showing that the word can refer not only to the sound itself but also to the audible expression being heard. It occurs 506 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force is shaped by the sentence and surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “cinnamon,” referring to a fragrant spice or aromatic substance. In the Old Testament, it appears three times: once in Exodus and twice in Proverbs and Song of Solomon. Its uses place it among valuable ingredients associated with fragrance, perfumed preparations, and pleasant scent. The word names the spice itself rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its use there.

This Hebrew word means “cold,” describing low temperature or the absence of warmth. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, with the same basic sense reflected in its recorded English renderings. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what is being described, but the central idea remains physical coldness rather than warmth. The word appears in Proverbs and Jeremiah, including Proverbs 25:25 and Jeremiah 18:14.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses “hearing” or doing something “diligently.” It concerns attentive listening or careful attention in a sentence, rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in three verses. Its uses are connected with hearing and speech, while one occurrence is rendered “diligently,” showing that its role can extend from listening to carrying something out attentively. The exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to a “glede,” a specific creature identified by name. Its precise role in the verse depends on the surrounding context, but the available meaning points to this single noun rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 14:13. The word therefore has a narrow, concrete sense in the biblical text rather than a broad range of repeated uses.

This Hebrew word means “spirit.” It refers to spirit as a distinct subject within the Old Testament language represented here. It appears eleven times, all in Daniel, including chapters 2, 4, 5, and later in the book. Thus, its use is not confined to one passage or setting. The word’s precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central lexical meaning remains “spirit.”

e.t: Ram is a personal name. In the Old Testament, it identifies people listed in family records and genealogies, including ancestors connected with the lines recorded in Ruth and 1 Chronicles. The name also identifies a person mentioned in Job. Because every recorded occurrence is rendered “Ram,” this word functions as a name rather than a general description or action. It occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, chiefly in genealogical passages.

This Hebrew word refers to a demand: something required or insisted upon. It functions as a term for what is being demanded rather than describing the person making the demand or the action of demanding. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 4:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense is a demand made or required.

This Hebrew word means “full.” It describes a state or condition rather than an action, presenting someone or something as full. The word occurs 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic sense appears across several passages rather than belonging to only one setting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Shillem is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Shillem” in the English Bible. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in Genesis 46:24 and once in Numbers 26:49. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further meaning beyond identifying the person called Shillem.

This word refers to “Samaritans,” functioning as a plural name for a people. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Kings 17:29. As a people-name, it identifies the group being spoken of rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic lexical meaning is the name of this people group.

This Hebrew word functions as the verb “are,” linking a subject with a description or condition. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 16:6, so its normal use cannot be illustrated through a broad range of passages. As a verb, “are” states that the subject stands in the condition expressed by the accompanying words. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described.

This Hebrew word refers to an occasion or a particular opportunity or circumstance. In English, it is rendered as “an” and “occasion,” functioning as a noun that identifies a specific occasion. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 14:4 and Jeremiah 2:24. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense points to an occasion or circumstance rather than a person, action, or quality.

e.t: “Thummim” is the name of a sacred object connected with Israel’s priesthood. It appears in the Old Testament as a distinct noun rather than as an ordinary descriptive word. The word is associated with the priestly breastpiece in Exodus and Leviticus, with the priestly office in Deuteronomy, and with decisions about priestly service after the exile in Ezra and Nehemiah. It occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and Scripture preserves the name without providing a fuller ordinary-language definition.

This Hebrew word means “Bow.” It functions as a command or public call for people to lower themselves in submission or honor. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 41:43. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s full force in that passage cannot be described more specifically. Its basic sense is a direct summons to bow before someone recognized as having authority or elevated status.

Etham is a proper name for a place mentioned in the Israelites’ journey. It is rendered “Etham” and occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in Exodus and three times in Numbers. The passages record Etham among the places associated with Israel’s movements and encampments, including the route described in Numbers 33. As a place name, the word identifies a location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea.

This Hebrew word means “medicine,” referring to something used to treat illness or restore health. It functions as a noun, naming a remedy rather than describing an action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 47:12. Its ordinary sense is therefore focused and specific: a medicinal treatment or healing substance. The surrounding verse provides the context for how this remedy is being described there.
